wine.name: Montefalco Sagrantino 25 Anni
wine.classification: DOCG, granted to Montefalco Sagrantino in 1992
wine.grapes: Sagrantino alone, as the DOCG requires, from the estate's own vineyards around Montefalco.
wine.sites: Several of the estate's own Sagrantino vineyards around Montefalco, on limestone and clay by the importer's sheets; the label names no single site.
wine.making: The grapes ferment in stainless steel with native yeasts and stay on their skins for about a month, by the importer's sheets. The house's own sheet then gives 24 months in French oak barriques and at least eight months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Blackberry jam, black cherry and ink over rose, nutmeg, cocoa and a note of tar; opaque, full bodied and warm, with dense tannin that dries the mouth like strong tea, fresh acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Hard and closed for its first years, it wants a decade to soften, and the house gives it a life of more than twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle needs two hours in a decanter, an old one careful decanting off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The DOCG of Sagrantino alone from the hills of Montefalco, made dry or as a sweet passito.
Twenty five years: the wine marked the estate's quarter century, first made with the 1993 vintage.

label.term: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
label.means: Italy's guaranteed tier, granted to Montefalco Sagrantino by a decree of 5 November 1992.

records.table: To mark the estate's twenty fifth year, Arnaldo Caprai first made its Montefalco Sagrantino 25 Anni with the 1993 vintage: Sagrantino alone, two years in French barriques. Inky, dark and fiercely tannic, it softens over a decade; decanted, it takes on red meat.
records.story: When Arnaldo Caprai, a textile manufacturer of Foligno who died in 2026 at the age of 92, bought land at Montefalco in 1971, the Val di Maggio estate with a little vineyard already planted among it, Sagrantino was close to vanishing, known mostly as a sweet passito. His son took over the running of the estate in the second half of the 1980s and turned it towards research: the house worked with the University of Milan on the clonal selection of Sagrantino, on new vineyards and on the grape's tannins, and in 2003 three clones it had selected entered Italy's national register of vine varieties. Montefalco Sagrantino, a DOC since 1979, was raised to DOCG by a decree of 5 November 1992. 25 Anni, first made with the 1993 vintage and released in 1996 for the estate's twenty fifth year, set out the results of that first decade of work in the vineyard and the cellar, and it carried dry Sagrantino onto wine lists abroad. The founder was made a Cavaliere del Lavoro in 2003. The wine puts modern dry Sagrantino in the glass: a grape of enormous tannin, tamed by ripeness and small French oak.

others.name: Montefalco Sagrantino Collepiano
others.note: The house's classic dry Sagrantino, made in the same DOCG as 25 Anni.

others.name: Montefalco Sagrantino Passito
others.note: The sweet form from dried grapes, the way Sagrantino was made before the dry wine.

traps: 25 Anni marks the estate's twenty fifth year, not the age of its vines or its time in oak: it was first made with the 1993 vintage.
Montefalco Sagrantino is Sagrantino alone; Montefalco Rosso is a Sangiovese led red with only a share of Sagrantino.
Dry Sagrantino is the modern style: the grape was long made as a sweet passito, which shares the same DOCG.

cards.front: Before release, how many months does Arnaldo Caprai's 25 Anni spend in oak and in bottle?
cards.back: 24 months in French oak barriques, then at least eight months in bottle, by the house's sheet.

cards.front: Which university worked with Arnaldo Caprai on Sagrantino's clones from the late 1980s?
cards.back: The University of Milan; three clones the estate selected entered Italy's national register in 2003.

questions.q: What goes into Arnaldo Caprai's Montefalco Sagrantino 25 Anni?
opts: Sagrantino alone
Sangiovese with a share of Sagrantino
Sagrantino with Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon
Sagrantino with a little Montepulciano
questions.exp: Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG must be Sagrantino alone; Sangiovese with a share of Sagrantino is Montefalco Rosso, a different wine of the same hills.

questions.q: Why is Arnaldo Caprai's Sagrantino called 25 Anni?
opts: It marked the estate's twenty fifth year
Its vines were twenty five years old
It spends twenty five months in oak
It was the zone's twenty fifth DOCG wine
questions.exp: Released in 1996, twenty five years after the estate was bought in 1971, it marked that anniversary; its time in oak is 24 months, not 25.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, and four more on the Montefalco Sagrantino rules shared with Paolo Bea (one, restricted to the consorzio's domain, found nothing); one fetch of the estate's history page was refused (its host does not resolve from here) and never retried. The DOC of 30 October 1979 and the DOCG of 5 November 1992 come from the region's consolidated disciplinare and the ministry's catalogue, read through search; the catalogue's address is http only and is not cited.

Arnaldo Caprai died on 4 or 5 January 2026 at 92 by wein.plus, Doctorwine, Gambero Rosso, La Nazione and Scatti di Gusto; one account gives his birth as Turin in 1933 and no second does, so he carries his death alone, and his textile business and funeral are at Foligno.

The fermentation in steel with native yeasts, the month on the skins and the clay and limestone rest on the American importer's fact sheets for several vintages, which relay the house's own data; the house's sheet read through search gives only the 24 months in barrique and eight in bottle and the life of over twenty years.

The house's pages give 1993 as the first vintage and 1996 as the release for the twenty fifth year; a sustainability report calls the 1996 edition the first made wholly of Sagrantino under a named consultant, a claim on one source left out.
The house's documents date the start of the work with the University of Milan to 1987 on one page and 1989 to 1990 on another, hence the late 1980s; the son is not named because he is living.

A Gambero Rosso headline speaks of an acquisition of the estate by Angelini Wine Estates, not read for want of searches; the record names no owner and tells no present ownership, and the refuter may add the sale as history if two sources date it.
The library record agrees; its trap on the historic passito is kept, and its glass note of tea is used in the glass.

changed: wine.sites: "on clay and limestone by the importer's sheet; unlike the house's Valdimaggio, drawn from the single Vigna del Lago, 25 Anni names no one site."; now "on limestone and clay by the importer's sheets; the label names no single site.": No source of the refuter's names a Vigna del Lago, and the author cited none for it: a search on the house's Valdimaggio and the vineyard found only a Valdimaggio first made, by one merchant listing, with the 2012 vintage, and nothing tying it to one vineyard. The comparison goes; the limestone and clay stand on the importer's sheets for two vintages.

others.2: "Valdimaggio: A Montefalco Sagrantino from the single Vigna del Lago, aged two years in French barriques."; now "(taken out; the others are Collepiano and the Passito, both the library's)": The single vineyard rests on no source read, and the two years in barrique on one merchant listing; with the vineyard gone the note would teach nothing a guest could keep.

story: "bought the Val di Maggio estate at Montefalco in 1971, with a little vineyard already planted, and added neighbouring land to grow Sagrantino. The grape was then close to vanishing,"; now "bought land at Montefalco in 1971, the Val di Maggio estate with a little vineyard already planted among it. Sagrantino was then close to vanishing,": The house's history page, read through search, says the textile entrepreneur bought land at Montefalco in 1971, the Val di Maggio estate among it with a few hectares already under vine (four on one page, three on another, so no figure); no source read says he then added neighbouring land to grow Sagrantino. The next sentence names the grape, which the cut clause had named before it.

story: "His son took the estate over in 1986 and turned it towards research: from the late 1980s the house worked with"; now "His son took over the running of the estate in the second half of the 1980s and turned it towards research: the house worked with": The house's history page dates the son's arrival at the helm to 1986, another page of the house to 1987, and the importer's story and a merchant's profile to 1988; the three agree on the second half of the decade and on nothing narrower. The late 1980s of the university work then goes from the sentence, which would say the decade twice; the card keeps it, on the house's 1987 and another source's 1990.

story: "The founder was made a Cavaliere del Lavoro for his services to agriculture in 2003."; now "The founder was made a Cavaliere del Lavoro in 2003.": The federation's list of those named in 2003 carries him, and the obituaries give the honour from President Ciampi on 2 June 2003; no source read gives the sector he was named for, and he was a textile manufacturer before he was a grower, so agriculture is cut.
open: La Nazione and Gambero Rosso report that the Angelini group's wine arm bought a majority of Arnaldo Caprai; no date was found in the summaries, so the sale is not told. The integrator may add it as history once a year is on two sources.
The 1979 DOC is told as Montefalco Sagrantino's, though the wine was then called Sagrantino di Montefalco and many labels still print that name; Wikipedia alone gives a change of name in 2009.
The release in 1996 rests on the importer's page and the house's pages as the author read them; the refuter read 1993 as the first vintage on the house's own page and on Decanter.

wine.name: Montefalco Sagrantino Pagliaro
wine.classification: DOCG, Italy's guaranteed tier, in its dry or secco type
wine.grapes: Sagrantino alone, as the DOCG requires, from the family's own vines.
wine.sites: The Pagliaro vineyard, a single hillside of the family's at Montefalco at about 400 metres above sea level, farmed without synthetic chemicals.
wine.making: It ferments with wild yeasts and stays on its skins for some six weeks or more, then ages a year or more in stainless steel, two years or more in large Slavonian oak casks and about a year in bottle. It is neither fined nor filtered, and sulphur, if any, goes in only at bottling.
wine.glass: Dried plum, black cherry and blackberry over balsamic herbs, iron filings, cured meat and dusty earth; brooding and savoury, sometimes cloudy, with a dense wall of tannin and fresh acidity that carry it long.
wine.ageing: Released some four years after the harvest and firm even then, it opens over the following decade and, kept cool, lasts many years beyond; bottles vary from one to the next.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; stand the bottle upright a day ahead and decant it gently off its deposit, for it is unfiltered; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The DOCG of Sagrantino alone from the hills of Montefalco, dry or passito; labels also print it as Sagrantino di Montefalco.
Dry: the word that sets this wine apart from the sweet Passito of the same DOCG.
The single vineyard on the family's hillside at Montefalco that gives the wine.

records.table: Wild yeasts, weeks on the skins and years in steel, large oak and bottle, never filtered: that is Paolo Bea's Sagrantino Pagliaro, a single vineyard Montefalco Sagrantino. Dark, savoury and wild, it asks to be eased off its deposit and poured with slow braised meat.
records.story: Documents in the village archives, as the family tells it, place the Bea family at Montefalco from the 1500s, and over the centuries the farm kept animals and grew olives and other crops beside its vines. The farm first bottled wine under its own name in 1980. The father whose name the farm carries held to a way of working that has defined the house: nothing synthetic in the vineyard, wild yeasts, macerations of six weeks and more, no fining, no filtering and late release. Sagrantino, long made as a sweet passito, won a DOC in 1979 and then the DOCG of 1992, which covers it dry and passito alike, and Pagliaro, the family's single vineyard dry Sagrantino, became the house's flagship. The son, trained as an architect, came home to run the cellar with his family. Pagliaro is as far from barrique aged Sagrantino as the zone allows: Montefalco's natural wine reference, made slowly, with nothing added beyond sulphur, if any, at bottling.

others.name: Rosso de Véo
others.note: The house's red of Sagrantino sold as an IGT, apart from the DOCG.

others.name: Arboreus
others.note: Trebbiano Spoletino from vines trained up trees in the old way, given long contact with its skins.

others.name: Montefalco Sagrantino Passito
others.note: Sagrantino's sweet side, from dried grapes, within the same DOCG.

traps: Bea's Pagliaro is a dry Montefalco Sagrantino, Secco on the label; the house's Passito is the sweet wine of the same DOCG.
Bea's Arboreus is Trebbiano Spoletino, and the shared name does not make it Trebbiano Toscano.
Some Bea bottlings appear as IGT rather than DOCG, so the label, not the house, tells you the category.

cards.front: What ageing does Paolo Bea's Sagrantino Pagliaro go through before release?
cards.back: About a year in stainless steel, two years or more in large Slavonian oak casks, then about a year in bottle, unfiltered.

cards.front: Since when has the Bea family farmed at Montefalco, and when did its farm first bottle wine?
cards.back: Since the 1500s, by the village archives as the family tells it; the farm first bottled its own wine in 1980.

questions.q: A guest finds a deposit in Paolo Bea's Montefalco Sagrantino Pagliaro and a slight haze in the glass. What explains it?
opts: It is bottled unfined and unfiltered
It was aged in new French barriques
It was made from dried grapes
It was fermented with cultured yeasts
questions.exp: The family fines and filters nothing, so a deposit is the house style, not a fault; wine from dried grapes is the sweet Passito, not Pagliaro.

questions.q: When did the farm behind Paolo Bea first bottle wine under its own name?
questions.exp: The farm first bottled its own wine in 1980, though by the family's account the village archives place it at Montefalco from the 1500s.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, plus the four on the Montefalco Sagrantino rules shared with Arnaldo Caprai, which give the DOC of 30 October 1979 and the DOCG of 5 November 1992; the house's pages read through search hold no sheet for Pagliaro itself, so its making rests on Wine-Searcher and on merchants' sheets that agree with it (about 40 to 50 days on the skins, a year in steel, two in large Slavonian oak, a year in bottle).
The vineyard at about 400 metres rests on two merchants (1,300 feet and 400 metres); one merchant's clay and gravel stands alone and is left out, and no aspect is given.
The label: merchants print both Montefalco Sagrantino Secco Pagliaro and Montefalco Sagrantino Pagliaro, so the name keeps the plan's words and Secco is taught as a label term.

The family's living members are not named: the father whose name the farm carries, his son trained as an architect (two sources) and another member said to farm the vines; the cellar the son designed of stone, wood and earth, and the year 1973 for the farm's registration, each rest on one source and are left out.

Rosso de Véo is told as the library tells it, an IGT red of Sagrantino; the house's page, read through search, adds the Cerrete vineyard at 400 to 430 metres on clay, left out for want of room among the five sources.
The importer most linked with the house is named for a living person and is never cited.
The library's and the region record's sweet passito for the church calendar or feast days is not in a source read here, so the story says only that Sagrantino was long made as a sweet passito.

changed: story: "and the farm grew grain and olives beside its vines."; now "and the farm kept animals and grew olives and other crops beside its vines.": The sources read describe a mixed farm of crops, orchards and animals, one of them with cattle as its main business and wine and olive oil made for the family and for local sale; grain alone was the library's word and too narrow.

story: "Sagrantino, long made as a sweet passito, became a dry wine of the Montefalco Sagrantino DOC of 1979 and then of the DOCG of 1992,"; now "Sagrantino, long made as a sweet passito, won a DOC in 1979 and then the DOCG of 1992, which covers it dry and passito alike,": The DOC dates from the presidential decree of 30 October 1979, under the name Sagrantino di Montefalco, and the DOCG of 5 November 1992 is reserved to a red in the types Secco and Passito; the old wording gave the DOC a name it did not then carry and made the DOC the moment Sagrantino became dry, which no source says.

wine.label.0.means: "The DOCG of Sagrantino alone from the hills of Montefalco, made dry or as a sweet passito."; now "The DOCG of Sagrantino alone from the hills of Montefalco, dry or passito; labels also print it as Sagrantino di Montefalco.": Merchants listing the bottle print Pagliaro Secco Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG as often as Montefalco Sagrantino, so a guest who meets either name on the label is told they are one DOCG.

wine.making: "then aged about a year in stainless steel,"; now "then aged a year or more in stainless steel,": Most merchants give about a year in steel, and one gives twelve to twenty four months; a year or more holds both.
open: Whether Bea's own label prints Montefalco Sagrantino or Sagrantino di Montefalco was not seen on the bottle; merchants print both, and the record now teaches both.
Farmed without synthetic chemicals rests on the author's secondaries (Grape Collective, Wine-Searcher) and was not re-searched.
Whether the father whose name the farm carries is living was not settled; he is not named, and the house keeps its name.

records.place: Torgiano, Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG, Umbria

wine.name: Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio
wine.classification: DOCG, the guaranteed designation, granted to Torgiano Rosso Riserva in 1990
wine.grapes: Sangiovese alone by the house's sheet for the 2020 vintage; the house's own accounts of older vintages give a share of Canaiolo.
wine.sites: The Monticchio vineyard on the Brufa hill above Torgiano, at about 300 metres and facing west south west, on soils of old lake origin: clay in layers with sand, the sand more frequent lower down.
wine.making: The house's sheet for the 2020 vintage gives a fermentation in stainless steel with some four weeks on the skins, about twelve months in fine grained oak, partly barriques and partly large casks, then about three years in bottle at the house before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, dried rose and violet over tobacco, leather and a touch of liquorice; medium to full in body, with bright acidity and firm, fine tannin that turns silky and savoury with age.
wine.ageing: Its years in bottle at the house leave it drinkable from release, and it lasts for decades; the house says it can go well beyond fifty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; air a young bottle in a decanter for an hour, and take an old one gently off its sediment; a large tulip shaped glass.

label.means: The house's name for its Torgiano red, from the Latin for to blush, first used for the 1962 vintage.
The single vineyard on the Brufa hill above Torgiano that gives the Riserva.
Umbria's DOCG red from grapes of the commune of Torgiano, aged at least three years before release.

records.table: Lungarotti draws its Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio, a Torgiano Rosso Riserva, from one hillside at Brufa: Sangiovese, a year in oak, then years in bottle at the house. Sour cherry, leather and tobacco sit over firm, fine tannin; decant it before game or roast meat.
records.story: Rubesco, its name drawn from the Latin for to blush, was launched with the 1962 vintage by Giorgio Lungarotti, who died in 1999, and with the 1964 he made the first Riserva from the Monticchio vineyard on the Brufa hill above Torgiano. In 1968 Torgiano became a DOC for its red and its white, by the house's account one of the early DOCs of Italy. On 23 April 1974 he and his wife opened a wine museum in the village, the MUVIT, and the family foundation that runs it followed in 1987. By a presidential decree of 20 October 1990 Torgiano Rosso Riserva became a DOCG that reached back, the house says, to the 1983 vintage, and Vigna Monticchio became the wine of that DOCG, from grapes of the commune of Torgiano alone. The family carried the house on after the founder's death, and the Riserva rests at least three years in bottle in the house's own cellar before it is released. Learning Torgiano Rosso Riserva means learning this bottle: a DOCG built by one family, and a Sangiovese that shows how Umbria ages.

others.name: Rubesco Rosso di Torgiano
others.note: The house's Torgiano Rosso DOC, Sangiovese led, first made with the 1962 vintage.

others.name: San Giorgio
others.note: Cabernet Sauvignon and Sangiovese from the house's Torgiano vineyards, sold as Umbria IGT rather than under the DOC.

traps: Torgiano Rosso Riserva is DOCG; plain Torgiano Rosso, Rubesco among them, is DOC.
Rubesco is a name the house gave its Torgiano red, not a grape or a place; Vigna Monticchio is the vineyard that marks the Riserva.
Umbria's two DOCGs are Torgiano Rosso Riserva and Montefalco Sagrantino; Orvieto, for all its fame, is a DOC.

cards.front: Where does Lungarotti's Vigna Monticchio vineyard lie, and on what soil?
cards.back: On the Brufa hill above Torgiano, at about 300 metres, on clay of old lake origin layered with sand.

cards.front: Lungarotti's Torgiano Rosso Riserva became a DOCG by decree in which year?
cards.back: 1990, by a presidential decree of 20 October; Torgiano had been a DOC since 1968.

questions.q: By the house's sheet, how is Lungarotti's Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio aged before it is sold?
opts: About a year in oak, then three in bottle
Two years in new barriques, then sold
Six months in steel, then sold young
Five years in large chestnut casks
questions.exp: The 2020 sheet gives about twelve months in barriques and large casks, then about three years in bottle; the DOCG itself asks at least three years in all before release.

questions.q: Lungarotti's first Riserva from the Monticchio vineyard on the Brufa hill came from which vintage?
questions.exp: The first Vigna Monticchio was the 1964; 1962 was the first vintage of Rubesco, 1968 the year of Torgiano's DOC and 1990 that of the DOCG.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35.

The label order: the house's own sheet and page print Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio, as the region record does; the library writes Rubesco Vigna Monticchio Riserva, as do some merchants, and may wish to follow the house.

The grapes: the house's 2020 sheet gives Sangiovese alone, while a house press release on the vintages from 1969 speaks of a high share of Canaiolo, about three in ten; the library's Sangiovese with Canaiolo holds for older bottles, and the record says no figure.

Giorgio Lungarotti died on 16 April 1999 by the house; Decanter gives his age as 89 and another profile as 88, so his birth year is uncertain between 1910 and 1911 and he carries his death alone; his wife is not named, for no source read gives her dates, and his living daughters are not named.
founded is left empty: the house dates Rubesco's first vintage to 1962, a company history gives 1962 for the firm and another account the late 1950s for the modern winery.
The retroactive DOCG from the 1983 vintage and the ten years in bottle of old are the house's own accounts; the vineyard's size and the olive oil museum's year are left out as volatile or unsourced.
The second source for the DOC of 1968 and the first Riserva of 1964 is Wine Industry Advisor; a wine writer's site that also gives them is named for a living person and is not cited.

The Torgiano rule: the ministry's catalogue, read through search, gives at least three years of ageing with six months of them in bottle, but a regional file of 2021 proposed new terms and a decree of 3 July 2023 amended the disciplinare, so the record says only at least three years; the catalogue's address is http only and is not cited, and the ministry's page for the DOCG stands in its place.

changed: wine.making: "By the house's sheet for the 2020 vintage, the wine ages about twelve months in fine grained oak, partly barriques and partly large casks, then about three years in bottle at the house before release. By the house's account it was once held far longer, as much as ten years, before it was sold."; now "By the house's sheet for the 2020 vintage, the wine ferments in stainless steel with some four weeks on its skins, ages about twelve months in fine grained oak, partly barriques and partly large casks, then rests about three years in bottle at the house before release.": The house's 2020 sheet, read through search on its own domain, gives fermentation in steel at a controlled temperature with 25 to 28 days on the skins, about twelve months in fine grained barriques and casks of 50 to 55 hectolitres, then three years in bottle; the ten years of old rests on no source the refuter found: a search for it returned bottle ageing of three to five years by vintage (the 2016 at least three, the 2011 sixty months by a merchant, the 2017 over forty), and none of ten.

story: "and it held the Riserva back in its own cellar for years before release, as long as a decade by its account, a period since shortened to about three years in bottle."; now "and the Riserva rests at least three years in bottle in the house's own cellar before it is released.": As in the making: the decade of old is in no source read, and the house's release notice for the 2016 and its 2020 sheet give at least three years in bottle before the wine leaves the cellar.

others.0: "Rubesco Torgiano Rosso: The house's Torgiano Rosso DOC, first made with the 1962 vintage, from Sangiovese with Canaiolo."; now "Rubesco Rosso di Torgiano: The house's Torgiano Rosso DOC, Sangiovese led, first made with the 1962 vintage.": The bottle is listed as Rubesco Rosso di Torgiano DOC by Falstaff and a merchant, the label's own order; its partner grape is Canaiolo in two sources and Colorino in another, so the note says Sangiovese led and names no second grape. The first vintage of 1962 stands on the house and two secondaries.

others.1.note: "A red of the house's Torgiano estate, sold as Umbria IGT rather than under the DOC."; now "Cabernet Sauvignon and Sangiovese from the house's Torgiano vineyards, sold as Umbria IGT rather than under the DOC.": The house's sheet and a merchant give Cabernet Sauvignon and Sangiovese in equal parts, Decanter adds a little Canaiolo; the two main grapes teach what the wine is, and the Umbria Rosso IGT is on all three.
open: Giorgio Lungarotti's birth year, 1910 in Wikipedia alone; he carries his death.
His wife, the art historian who co founded the museum and the foundation, died in November 2025 aged 99 by Gambero Rosso; with a second source for her dates she could be named in the story.
The day of the DOCG decree, 20 October 1990 in the disciplinare's text and 10 October in one secondary.
The share of Canaiolo in older vintages of Vigna Monticchio, which the author read in a house release and the refuter did not re-read; the grapes field says no figure.

records.place: The castle of Sala near Orvieto, Umbria IGT, Umbria

wine.name: Cervaro della Sala
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, the great majority, with a little Grechetto.
wine.sites: Vineyards around the castle, between about 200 and 400 metres, on clay soils rich in marine fossils, by the estate's sheet for the 2011 vintage.
wine.making: The Chardonnay is fermented in barriques and goes through a partial malolactic there, while the Grechetto is fermented apart in stainless steel. After some months in barrique the Chardonnay returns to steel to be blended with the Grechetto, and the wine is bottled and rested for months in the castle's old cellars before release.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, yellow apple and grapefruit over hazelnut, butter and toast, with a flinty, struck match edge; full and creamy, with fresh acidity to hold it up and a long finish of bitter almond.
wine.ageing: Good from two or three years after the vintage, it gains honeyed, nutty depth for a decade or longer in a good year.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; skip the decanter and let a young bottle open in the glass; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Named, by the estate's account, for the Monaldeschi della Cervara, a noble family of the castle's past.
The regional category of Umbria, wider than a DOC, under which the estate sells this Chardonnay led white.
The fourteenth century castle near Orvieto that the Antinori family bought in 1940.

records.table: The Antinori family's castle near Orvieto, Castello della Sala, first made Cervaro della Sala in 1985: Chardonnay fermented in barriques, with a little Grechetto from steel. Rich, toasty and fresh, it meets white meats or truffled pasta, poured cool rather than icy.
records.story: A lord of the Monaldeschi, a noble family of Orvieto whose four branches long feuded, built the castle in 1350, by the estate's account; in the later fifteenth century a marriage with a cousin of the Monaldeschi della Cervara, one of those branches, ended the feud, and the wine takes its name from that line. In 1940 the castle was bought by the Florentine Antinori family, wine merchants for centuries, whose marchese had launched the Villa Antinori label in 1928. The 1985 gave the first Cervaro della Sala: Chardonnay with a little Grechetto, the Chardonnay fermented in barriques. The house counts it among the first Italian wines to go through malolactic fermentation and ageing in barrique, and Muffato della Sala, its sweet sibling of noble rot, followed with the 1987. Labelled Umbria IGT rather than Orvieto, Cervaro is Chardonnay shaped by Grechetto, small barrels and the clay of a castle's hill.

others.name: Muffato della Sala
others.note: The estate's sweet white of grapes touched by noble rot and picked in several passes, first made in 1987 and sold as Umbria IGT.

traps: Cervaro della Sala is sold as Umbria IGT, not as Orvieto DOC: Orvieto's rules are built on Grechetto and Trebbiano, and Cervaro is mostly Chardonnay.
Castello della Sala is the Antinori family's Umbrian estate; Tignanello and Solaia come from its Tuscan vineyards in Chianti Classico.
The name Cervaro comes from the Monaldeschi della Cervara, a noble family of the castle, not from a grape or a vineyard.

cards.front: How are the two grapes of Cervaro della Sala fermented?
cards.back: The Chardonnay in barriques, with a partial malolactic; the Grechetto apart in stainless steel; the two are blended in steel some months later.

cards.front: When did the Antinori family buy Castello della Sala, and what was the first vintage of Cervaro?
cards.back: The castle in 1940; the first Cervaro della Sala was the 1985.

An old local name for the Grechetto grape
questions.exp: The estate says the name honours the Monaldeschi della Cervara, a line of the noble family that held the castle in its past; the Antinori family bought it only in 1940.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35, plus two on the Orvieto disciplinare shared with Barberani; the house's pages, read through search, are primary for its own dates, sites and making, and merchants agree on the purchase of 1940 and the 1985.

No source read gives the dates of the marchese who bought the castle, so he is described by the Villa Antinori he created in 1928; the castle's medieval lords are described too, for want of their dates; the winemaker who came in 1979 is living and not named.

The estate's pages put the marriage that ended the feud in 1466 on one page and 1480 on another, and the Cervara line's tenure in the fourteenth century on one and the sixteenth on another, so the story gives neither year.

The blend is given as about nine parts Chardonnay to one of Grechetto by merchants, with the 1985 at about four to one, hence the great majority; the time in barrique moves from about three to six months by vintage and is left out.
founded is empty: the castle dates from the fourteenth century and the family's purchase from 1940, and neither is a founding of the wine estate.
The Muffato and Pinot Nero notes rest on the estate's own wine pages and merchants; their grapes beyond Pinot Noir are left out, as sources list them differently.
The house is not in the library; the region record's line agrees.

changed: story: "a noble family of Orvieto whose branches long feuded, and in 1437 his grandson, the first to call himself della Sala, took power in Orvieto for ten years. A marriage with a cousin of the Monaldeschi della Cervara later ended the feud between the family's branches, and the wine takes its name from that line."; now "a noble family of Orvieto whose four branches long feuded, and in the later fifteenth century a marriage with a cousin of the Monaldeschi della Cervara, one of those branches, ended the feud; the wine takes its name from that line.": The castle of 1350 and its builder of the Monaldeschi stand on the estate's page and an Italian museum listing; the four branches, the della Cervara among them, on Wikipedia's Monaldeschi entry; the reconciling marriage is after 1466 on the estate's page and in 1480 in the museum listing and Wikipedia, so the later fifteenth century. The grandson's seizure of Orvieto in 1437 and his being the first to call himself della Sala rest on one page of the estate's, a claim of a first on one source, and are cut.

story: "After 1861 the castle passed through many hands, and in 1940 it was bought by the Florentine Antinori family, wine merchants for centuries, through the marchese who had created its Villa Antinori in 1928. The estate's winemaker came to Sala in 1979, and after a run of trial vintages that did not satisfy the house, the 1985 gave the first Cervaro della Sala:"; now "In 1940 the castle was bought by the Florentine Antinori family, wine merchants for centuries, whose marchese had launched the Villa Antinori label in 1928. The 1985 gave the first Cervaro della Sala:": The purchase of 1940 is on the estate's pages and Wikipedia, and the Villa Antinori label of 1928 by the marchese on two of the house's pages; that this marchese made the purchase, the many hands after 1861, the winemaker's arrival in 1979 and the trial vintages were in none of the refuter's results, a search for the arrival on the house's domain returning nothing, so they go. The winemaker is living and was never named.

story: "By the house's account it was among the first Italian whites to go through malolactic fermentation and age in barrique. Labelled Umbria IGT, it is the Umbrian white"; now "By the house's account it was one of the first Italian wines to go through malolactic fermentation and ageing in barrique, and Muffato della Sala, its sweet sibling of noble rot, followed with the 1987. Labelled Umbria IGT, Cervaro is the Umbrian white": The house's claim is put in its own words (one of the first Italian wines to have malolactic fermentation and ageing in barrique), not narrowed to whites; Muffato's first vintage of 1987 is on the house's own vintage page, which brings the story back over its floor after the cuts and names the estate's other wine a guest meets.

wine.making: "In February the Chardonnay returns to steel to be blended with the Grechetto,"; now "After some months in barrique the Chardonnay returns to steel to be blended with the Grechetto,": The house's vintage pages differ: February on some, after about three months on the 2015 page and six months on the fine lees on the 2012 page, so no month is given.
cards.0.back: "the two are blended in February."; now "the two are blended in steel some months later.": As in the making: the month moves with the vintage.

questions.1.exp: "The estate says the name honours the Monaldeschi della Cervara, the noble line joined to the castle's lords by marriage; the Antinori family bought the castle only in 1940."; now "The estate says the name honours the Monaldeschi della Cervara, a line of the noble family that held the castle in its past; the Antinori family bought it only in 1940.": The house's wine pages say the name comes from the Monaldeschi della Cervara who held the castle (in the fourteenth century on one page, the sixteenth on another); the old explanation made them only in laws by marriage.

others.0.note: "The estate's sweet white of late picked grapes touched by noble rot, sold as Umbria IGT."; now "The estate's sweet white of grapes touched by noble rot and picked in several passes, first made in 1987 and sold as Umbria IGT.": The house's vintage pages give the first Muffato as the 1987 and the picking by hand in a series of passes as the rot appears; the grapes are left out, as the author left them, for the blend moves by vintage.
open: The claim that Cervaro was one of the first Italian wines with malolactic fermentation and ageing in barrique is the house's alone, hedged as its account.
The century of the Monaldeschi della Cervara at the castle, the fourteenth or the sixteenth by the house's own pages; the record names neither.
The sites rest on the house's 2011 sheet as the author read it.

records.place: Baschi, by Lake Corbara, Orvieto Classico, Umbria

wine.name: Orvieto Classico Superiore Muffa Nobile Calcaia
wine.classification: Classico and Superiore within the Orvieto DOC, in its Muffa Nobile type
wine.grapes: Grechetto and Procanico, as Trebbiano Toscano is called at Orvieto, at its heart; some vintages add other white grapes, and the shares move with the year.
wine.sites: Organically farmed hillside vineyards above Lake Corbara, the reservoir on the Tiber near Baschi, where autumn morning mists off the water bring noble rot.
wine.making: Pickers pass through the vines by hand five or six times in the autumn, taking only the bunches the noble rot has reached. The must ferments with its own yeasts in temperature controlled stainless steel and matures for some months before it is bottled in 50 centilitre bottles.
wine.glass: Apricot, candied orange peel and saffron over acacia honey, white almond and citrus blossom; golden and sweet, yet nimble for its sugar, lifted by fresh acidity to a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Charming in its first few years, it deepens towards marmalade and dried apricot over ten years and more.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, with no decanter, in a small white wine glass, beside blue cheese or a fruit tart.

label.means: Noble rot: a type the Orvieto DOC names, for sweet wine from botrytised grapes.
From the historic heart of the Orvieto zone around the town, its original area.
Orvieto of higher minimum natural alcohol, held back until the spring after the harvest.

records.table: Autumn mists off Lake Corbara bring the noble rot to the organic vines behind Barberani's Calcaia, a sweet Orvieto Classico Superiore. Golden and honeyed, with apricot and saffron, yet light on its feet; chill it well and bring blue cheese.
records.story: Barberani was founded in 1961 in the Classico heart of Orvieto, on the hills that fall to Lake Corbara, the reservoir on the Tiber below the town, and the family farms its vines organically. Orvieto became a DOC by a decree of 7 August 1971, for whites of Grechetto and of Trebbiano, which the growers here call Procanico. The rules name a Muffa Nobile type, for sweet wine from grapes taken by noble rot, and the lake gives the conditions for it: morning mists in autumn, then breezy, sunny afternoons that dry the berries and concentrate their sugar. Calcaia is the house's answer, picked by hand in five or six passes through the autumn and fermented in steel. It is made as a Sauternes is made, by noble rot, yet it tastes lighter and fresher. Luigi Barberani, the founder's son, who led the house for decades, died in October 2025. Calcaia is Orvieto's sweet side, set against its dry whites: noble rot that a lake brings about in central Italy.

others.name: Orvieto Classico Superiore Castagnolo
others.note: A dry Orvieto Classico Superiore of the house, from its organic vines above the lake.

traps: Calcaia is a Muffa Nobile, sweet from noble rot; abboccato and amabile on an Orvieto label are lighter grades of sweetness, a different style.
Procanico is no grape of its own: it is the Orvieto name for Trebbiano Toscano.
Lake Corbara is a reservoir on the Tiber below Orvieto, not Lake Trasimeno or Lake Bolsena.

cards.front: What brings noble rot to the vines of Barberani's Calcaia?
cards.back: Autumn morning mists off Lake Corbara, then breezy, sunny afternoons that dry the berries and concentrate their sugar.

cards.front: On Barberani's Calcaia label, what do Classico and Superiore promise?
cards.back: Classico: the historic heart of the Orvieto zone; Superiore: higher minimum natural alcohol and a release held until the spring after the harvest.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, plus the two on the Orvieto disciplinare shared with Castello della Sala, for 33 of the group's 35 in all; the house's own site returned nothing to a search restricted to its domain, so the record's one primary is the Orvieto disciplinare (the Muffa Nobile type, Classico and Superiore in the region's consolidated text, the decree of 7 August 1971 in the ministry's catalogue, whose address is http only and is not cited), and every other fact rests on two secondaries.

Calcaia's first vintage is left out: an encyclopedia entry dates the first bottle of the house's Muffa Nobile to 1986 and Gambero Rosso the first Calcaia to 1991, and the plan's note gave 1981 or 1986.

The founding of 1961 rests on Vinexus, a merchant directory and Doctorwine; Doctorwine alone names the founder and gives Luigi Barberani's age at death as 87, so the founder is not named and Luigi carries only his death in October 2025, which Gambero Rosso and Startmag report.

The grapes: the Wine Society gives Trebbiano Toscano and Grechetto and a merchant Grechetto and Procanico, the same pair; a Wine Enthusiast note of the 2007 adds Sauvignon Blanc, so the record says the shares move with the year and names no third grape.

The organic farming rests on the Wine Society's organic listings and a merchant; the reviewer who lists its certification is named for a living person and is not cited; the hand picking in passes and the steel rest on two merchants' sheets.
The family's living members, the founder's grandsons among them, are not named, nor is the dry Orvieto named for a living member of the family.
The house is not in the library; the region record's line agrees.

The disciplinare had a temporary amendment by decree of 8 August 2024 and an ordinary one sent to the European Commission on 8 July 2025, so the Superiore terms are told without the figures (11.5 per cent natural alcohol and release after 1 March, by the older text) that may move.

changed: wine.grapes: "Grechetto with Procanico, as Trebbiano Toscano is called at Orvieto, in shares that move with the year."; now "Grechetto and Procanico, as Trebbiano Toscano is called at Orvieto, at its heart; some vintages add other white grapes, and the shares move with the year.": Grechetto and Trebbiano or Procanico are on the Wine Society's and a merchant's listings, but a merchant's breakdown of the 2019 adds Verdello and Wine Enthusiast's note of the 2007 adds Sauvignon Blanc, so the old wording, which read as the pair alone, now says other white grapes come in some years and names none.

wine.sites: "near Baschi, at about 200 to 300 metres, where"; now "near Baschi, where": No source of the refuter's gives the vineyards' height, and the author cited none for it; the reservoir on the Tiber (the dam built from 1959 to 1963) and the autumn mists stand on the region's data, Wikipedia and the merchants.

wine.making: "Picked by hand in five or six passes from October, in some years into December, taking only the bunches the noble rot has reached. The must ferments with its own yeasts in temperature controlled stainless steel and matures for some months in the same tanks before it is bottled"; now "Picked by hand in five or six passes through the autumn, taking only the bunches the noble rot has reached. The must ferments with its own yeasts in temperature controlled stainless steel and matures for some months before it is bottled": The five or six passes by hand, the native yeasts and the temperature controlled steel stand on a merchant's sheet and the author's; a Gambero Rosso vertical has the botrytised grapes of 2008 picked in October; December and the maturing in the same tanks are in no source read, so the months are the autumn and the vessel of the maturing goes.

story: ", which the growers here call Procanico, the more generous cropper that growers long favoured over Grechetto."; now ", which the growers here call Procanico.": That Procanico is the more generous cropper growers long favoured is in no source read; Procanico as Trebbiano Toscano at Orvieto is in the EU's single document for the DOC.

story: "picked by hand in five or six passes from October, in hot years only in December when the rot comes late, and fermented in steel."; now "picked by hand in five or six passes through the autumn and fermented in steel.": As in the making: December in hot years is in no source read.

story: "Luigi Barberani, of the founding family and one of the known figures of Umbrian wine, died in October 2025."; now "Luigi Barberani, the founder's son, who led the house for decades, died in October 2025.": Gambero Rosso names the founder of 1961 as Luigi's father and a merchant has the father planting the first vines; Gambero Rosso dates the death to 22 October 2025 and Doctorwine reports it; Callmewine has Luigi and his wife running the house from the 1970s. The founder stays unnamed, for no source read gives his dates.
questions.0.exp: "in five or six passes from October,"; now "in five or six passes through the autumn,": As in the making.
open: Calcaia's first vintage, 1986 or 1991, and the plan's 1981, which no source gives.
The third and fourth grapes of Calcaia in some vintages (Verdello in one listing, Sauvignon Blanc in one note), named in no field.
The founder, named Vittorio in Gambero Rosso and by a merchant, has no dates in any source read and stays described.

The Superiore rules (higher natural alcohol, release from 1 March after the harvest in the older text) are told without figures, as the author told them, since the disciplinare was amended in 2023 and 2024.
